title: Beyond Words Per Minute
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Third-grade teacher Samantha Lippert describes two years of building an intentional fluency routine from scratch after recognizing she had never truly taught reading fluency systematically. Her core realization: fluency is not about speed but about freeing students to think -- automatic word recognition is the platform from which comprehension can launch. Her 10-minute weekly routine embeds fluency inside existing ELA instruction rather than adding a separate block: Monday introduces vocabulary pulled from the week's core ELA text (targeting cognates and key terms) plus echo reading and partner reading; Tuesday through Thursday students reread the same passage twice daily with partners while the teacher provides in-the-moment coaching to two or three target students without pulling anyone out; Friday students reread silently and answer comprehension questions styled after state assessment formats. Because passages tie directly to core ELA curriculum, a single routine simultaneously builds fluency, vocabulary, background knowledge, and assessment fluency. Cold reads vs. hot reads tracked separately reveal what a single benchmark score obscures: one student needed a different approach (transfer gap), another just needed time (rate gap). Lippert argues the routine extends to upper grades where fluency practice has largely disappeared.
points: * Fluency is not about speed -- it is about word recognition becoming automatic enough that working memory is freed to process meaning; the shift from labored to fluent reading opens the door to comprehension. * The weekly routine embeds 10 minutes of connected fluency practice inside the existing ELA block: vocabulary preview Monday, repeated partner reading Tue-Thu with embedded teacher coaching, comprehension check Friday. * Connecting fluency passages to the core curriculum text creates a reinforcing loop: vocabulary, background knowledge, comprehension, and fluency all strengthen simultaneously in the same ten minutes. * Cold reads (unfamiliar passages) and hot reads (practiced passages) tracked separately reveal what a single benchmark cannot: whether a student has a transfer gap, a rate gap, or simply needs more time. * The teacher is the intervention: 2-3 minutes of specific, immediate feedback within the routine during partner reading time often outperforms a separate pull-out block -- and the student never leaves the room or receives the message that they don't belong.
quotes: What changed my thinking was realizing that fluency is not really about speed. It's about freeing students to think.
When a student doesn't have to work hard to decode every word, their brain can do something more interesting: think about what they're reading!
You can hear fluency before you measure it.
in a lot of classrooms, the teacher is doing most of the reading.
Your presence is the intervention. Not a separate program. Not a worksheet.
Think of fluency as the Velcro -- it's what helps students connect the words on the page to the vocabulary, background knowledge, and genre understanding they're building all year.
Fluency isn't really about words per minute. It's about giving students enough automaticity to think deeply about what they read -- and enough time inside real reading to become readers.
